attempts.hypothesis: I believe this world rewards adaptive model-free driving with science-guided hunting of misplaced hints and strict energy/time accounting, so I ship a self-tuning differential-drive controller with hill-climbing site search, obstacle repulsion, stuck recovery and continuous trip-feasibility checks.
I’m treating hints and sensors as noisy, so I’m adding adaptive navigation, local site searches, and conservative return-to-base energy checks.
Compass and GPS faults are real, so I’m stabilizing navigation with wheel odometry and GPS course, searching noisy hints systematically, and making complete sampling-and-return trips the priority.

I believe the rover is being trapped by unreliable heading estimates and overly cautious task handling, so I’m using GPS/odometry calibration, compact hint coverage, and conservative sample-and-return planning.

The trace shows the rover spending nearly the whole mission issuing hold-like commands, so I’m replacing the fragile navigation gating with direct site approach, a compact hint-search sweep, and explicit return-safe driving.

The trace shows the rover settling into a hold after a brief departure, so I’m removing fragile task gating and using direct site approach, a bounded hint scan, and explicit sampling and return control.

I believe unreliable heading/GPS and overly broad hint searches caused the rover to wander without sampling; I’m using odometry with GPS/compass fault checks, compact site searches, and cautious sample-and-return trips.

I believe the tested sampling and navigation are sound, but returning with only a few samples and idling near the end wastes mission time, so I’m letting the rover keep searching when its return is feasible and giving it short endgame searches near base.
I believe the rover lost value by carrying samples through fruitless searches, so I’m restoring the proven three-sample and no-target return rules to enable another delivery run.

I infer a sparse-sensor differential-drive world with shifted hints, uncertain traction, and occasional sensor faults, so I’m building a cautious map-and-search controller that banks samples at the base and adapts speed/energy margins from observed battery use.

I’m replacing the overly complex first controller with a lighter, bounded planner plus robust odometry, obstacle recovery, adaptive charging/return logic, and science-guided local searches around survey hints.

The previous controller ignored nearly all survey targets because its energy model rejected them as too costly, so I’m replacing it with a conservative, low-speed rover that follows nearby hints, does short adaptive spirals for misplaced sites, samples opportunistically, and returns after each early

The previous run drove too slowly, returned after too few samples, and could get trapped against mapped/real obstacles for long periods; I’m switching to a faster batched collector with adaptive obstacle mapping, progress-based escape, local hint spirals, and a conservative time/energy return gate.

I’m keeping the controller conservative about faults but much more aggressive about collecting and batching samples, with adaptive map-building, faster travel, science-guided local search, and return logic based on measured energy use.

I’m replacing the heavy planner with a compact state machine that uses survey hints plus local spirals, reactive ray avoidance, conservative energy/time return gates, and adaptive wheel/compass/energy tracking to avoid last run’s controller errors.

The rover previously wasted time orbiting obstacles and aborted drilling too close to the 1.5 m limit, so I’m making drilling start with more margin, holding via site feedback, banking samples sooner, and adding local science-triggered searches plus stronger stuck/obstacle recovery.

The previous failures were trapped by idle local searches near the base; I’m replacing that with an explicit survey-hint state machine, larger but finite hint searches, robust slow drilling with hold control, and conservative energy/time return gates, plus basic grid/A* navigation for obstacles.

I assume a compass bias and noisy GPS, so the controller corrects heading from GPS course, searches a ring around misplaced hints, and returns to base when the load is full or time or battery runs short.

Attempt 1 delivered nothing because it never committed to returning to base, so I'm making delivery a firm goal, adding dead reckoning for GPS freezes, bounding each hint's search, and replacing the wall-clock-dependent stuck logic with wheel-speed and progress checks.

Attempt 2 averaged under 0.6 m/s and was slowed by wall-chasing and wasted hint searches, so I'm adding a faster speed-scaled obstacle steer, using the science signal to reject false hints and guide spiral searches, and keeping goals sticky.

Attempt 3 lost time because drills failed on slopes where the rover rolled back, and it crashed at 1 m/s into a rock. I'm keeping its goal and search logic but adding an integrating hold that actually stops the rover, a front-ray speed cap with braking, and a learned wheel-to-command gain.

Attempt 4's logs show the rover wedged for about 200 s in a reverse-recovery loop with zero wheel speed, plus a 70 s GPS freeze and oversized spiral searches; I'm replacing the reverse-only stall recovery with a cycling forward, pivot and reverse escape, exempting held positions from stall detection

The attempt-5 wedge was a loop of bump-triggered reverse nudges that never moved the rover, so this version uses one timed escape sequence (reverse, pivot, forward) that also charges a failed try to the current goal, plus a stuck detector and a goal-progress watchdog, while keeping the delivery and

Attempt 6 delivered 8 samples by about 500 s, then wandered for 150 s near a rock cluster and crashed at 1.1 m/s, so this version caps speed by the forward-cone clearance and makes exploration coverage-based.
I believe the 1.1 m/s rock crashes came from the forward speed cap being too loose, so this version keeps the attempt-6 mission logic and uses attempt 7's wider forward-cone speed limit.
